narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence and unfortunately pushed the prediction toward failure. Even though your 3.3 GPA is slightly above the average of accepted students (3.23), the model determined that this level of performance still signals a higher risk of struggling with the bar.

The next most important factor worked in your favor: your strong performance in the third year of law school. Placing in the 9th decile far exceeds the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this achievement pulled the prediction noticeably toward passing.

Your LSAT score of 40 was the third most influential element. While this is higher than the 37.2 average among accepted applicants, the model still viewed it as contributing to the risk of failure.

Taken together, the model concluded that your overall academic profile tilts toward a greater likelihood of not passing the bar on the first try.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Consider targeted bar-prep courses, especially those that build on undergraduate-level reasoning, and retake the LSAT if possible to raise your score further. With improved results in these key areas, your next application will have a much better chance of success. (248 words)
